question: Who does the manual say should attempt to carry passengers or large loads on a motorcycle?
choice_a: Any rider, regardless of experience level
choice_b: Only riders who have completed a three-wheel motorcycle course
choice_c: Only experienced riders, since the extra weight requires extra practice, preparation and caution
choice_d: Beginning riders specifically, to build confidence quickly
explanation: The manual states that because a passenger or cargo will affect how the motorcycle behaves, requiring extra practice, preparation and caution, only experienced riders should attempt to carry passengers or large loads.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Carrying Passengers and Cargo'

question: Before checking the headlight beam for a fully loaded trip, how should the motorcycle be positioned to mark the unloaded beam location?
choice_a: 50 feet from any wall in direct sunlight
choice_b: Headlight aim never needs adjustment regardless of load
choice_c: Directly against the wall with the engine off
choice_d: About 10 feet from a wall in an unlighted garage, marking the beam location with chalk
explanation: The manual instructs positioning the motorcycle about 10 feet from a wall in an unlighted garage and marking the headlight beam location with chalk before loading, then rechecking with a full load and passenger and adjusting the beam to match.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35, 'Preparing Your Motorcycle'

question: What personal protective gear should a passenger wear, according to the manual?
choice_a: The same level of personal protective gear as the operator
choice_b: No protective gear is necessary for passengers
choice_c: Only a helmet; other gear is optional for passengers
choice_d: Whatever the passenger happens to be wearing that day
explanation: The manual states that a passenger should be properly attired, wearing the same level of personal protective gear as the operator.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.35-36, 'Equipment for Carrying a Passenger'

question: Where should a child be seated on a motorcycle, and why?
choice_a: In front of the rider, so the rider can monitor them directly
choice_b: Immediately behind the rider -- a child in front cannot properly balance and may interfere with the rider's control
choice_c: Standing on the footrests without sitting down
choice_d: Seating position for children makes no difference to control or balance
explanation: The manual states that children should be placed immediately behind the rider, since a child sitting in front of the rider will not be able to properly balance and may interfere with the rider's control of the motorcycle.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.36, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: Why does the manual say riders should always instruct their passenger on cycling basics before a trip, even if the passenger already rides motorcycles?
choice_a: It is only necessary for first-time passengers who have never ridden before
choice_b: Passenger instruction is purely a formality with no safety purpose
choice_c: Riders should not assume passengers are familiar with this particular motorcycle's handling, control, or balance
choice_d: Only children need to be instructed before a ride
explanation: The manual advises that as a routine practice, riders should always instruct their passenger on cycling basics prior to starting the trip, even if the passenger is a motorcycle rider themselves, since riders should not assume passengers are familiar with this motorcycle's handling, control or balance.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.36, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: How should a passenger get on the motorcycle, according to the manual's instructions?
choice_a: Before the engine is started, so the passenger can get comfortable first
choice_b: While the motorcycle is in first gear with the clutch released
choice_c: It does not matter when the passenger mounts relative to starting the engine
choice_d: Only after the engine has been started and the transmission is in neutral, while the rider keeps both feet on the ground with the brakes applied
explanation: The manual instructs that a passenger should get on the motorcycle only after the rider has started the engine and put the transmission in neutral, keeping both feet on the ground and the brakes applied as the passenger mounts.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.36-37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: Why does the manual say a passenger should keep both feet firmly on the footrests even when the motorcycle is stopped?
choice_a: Firm footing prevents the passenger from falling off and pulling the rider off
choice_b: It is only a comfort consideration, not a safety one
choice_c: Footrests are only needed while the motorcycle is moving
choice_d: Passengers should instead place their feet on the ground whenever stopped
explanation: The manual instructs passengers to keep both feet firmly on the cycle's footrests even when stopped, since firm footing will prevent the passenger from falling off and pulling the rider off as well.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: What should a passenger do through turns and curves, according to the manual?
choice_a: Lean in the opposite direction of the turn to counterbalance the rider
choice_b: Stay directly behind the rider and lean with the rider, looking over the rider's shoulder in the direction of the turn
choice_c: Sit upright and rigid, refusing to lean at all
choice_d: Turn around to watch traffic behind during the turn
explanation: The manual instructs passengers to stay directly behind the rider and lean with the rider through turns and curves, and notes it is helpful for the passenger to look over the rider's shoulder in the direction of the turn.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: The manual instructs passengers to tighten their hold in which of these situations?
choice_a: Only when the passenger feels uncomfortable, without any specific trigger
choice_b: Only at highway speeds above 55 mph
choice_c: When approaching surface hazards, when the motorcycle is about to start from a stop, or when about to turn sharply or make a sudden move
choice_d: A passenger should never need to change their grip during a ride
explanation: The manual reminds passengers to tighten their hold when approaching surface hazards such as bumps, when about to start from a stop or begin moving into traffic, and when about to turn sharply or make a sudden move.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.37, 'Preparing Your Passenger to Ride'

question: How does carrying a passenger affect how quickly a motorcycle speeds up, slows down, or turns?
choice_a: Passenger weight has no measurable effect on these dynamics
choice_b: A heavier passenger makes the motorcycle speed up and turn faster
choice_c: Only slowing down is affected; acceleration and turning stay the same
choice_d: The heavier the passenger, the longer it will take to speed up, slow down, or turn
explanation: The manual explains that a motorcycle will respond differently with a passenger, and the heavier the passenger, the longer it will take to speed up, slow down, or turn.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.37-38, 'Riding With Passengers'

question: What warning does the manual give about riding through curves, corners, or bumps with a passenger if part of the motorcycle scrapes the ground?
choice_a: Steering control can be lost if any part of the motorcycle scrapes the ground at lean angle
choice_b: Scraping is purely cosmetic and has no effect on control
choice_c: Scraping only affects fuel economy, not handling
choice_d: It is impossible for a loaded motorcycle to scrape in a turn
explanation: The manual warns that when riding with passengers, riders should go a little slower through curves, corners, or bumps, because if any part of the motorcycle scrapes the ground at lean angle, steering control can be lost.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.38, 'Riding With Passengers'

question: What does the manual say about exceeding the gross vehicle weight rating when traveling with cargo and a passenger?
choice_a: The rating only applies to two-wheel motorcycles without passengers
choice_b: It should never be exceeded, and adjustments should always be made to the motorcycle to compensate for the added weight
choice_c: Exceeding the rating slightly is acceptable on short trips
choice_d: The gross vehicle weight rating is a suggestion, not a real limit
explanation: The manual instructs that riders should not exceed the gross vehicle weight rating when traveling with cargo and a passenger, and should always make adjustments to the motorcycle to compensate for the added weight.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.38, 'Carrying Loads'

question: Where does the manual recommend placing heavier cargo, and what problem can result from loading behind the rear axle?
choice_a: Heavier items should always go as far back as possible, behind the rear axle
choice_b: Load placement has no effect on handling as long as total weight is within limits
choice_c: Keep the load forward, over or in front of the rear axle -- mounting loads behind the rear axle can affect how the motorcycle turns and brakes, and can also cause a wobble
choice_d: All cargo should be strapped directly to the handlebars
explanation: The manual advises keeping the load forward and trying to place it over or in front of the rear axle, warning that mounting loads behind the rear axle can affect how the motorcycle turns and brakes, and can also cause a wobble.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.38, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: According to the manual, what is usually the peak performance window for most riders on a long trip, and what should they do afterward?
choice_a: Late evening, after most traffic has cleared for the day
choice_b: Peak performance time does not vary and riders should never take breaks
choice_c: Immediately after a large midday meal
choice_d: Starting as early as possible, usually between 6 a.m. and 11 a.m., then taking a good hour's break for lunch
explanation: The manual suggests starting as early in the morning as possible, since this is usually the peak performance window (typically 6 a.m. to 11 a.m.) for most riders, followed by a good hour's break for lunch.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: What does the manual recommend if you use saddlebags to carry cargo?
choice_a: Load each saddlebag with about the same weight, since an uneven load can cause the motorcycle to pull to one side
choice_b: Always load one side much heavier than the other for stability
choice_c: Saddlebags should only ever be used empty for aerodynamics
choice_d: Weight distribution between saddlebags does not matter
explanation: The manual advises loading each saddlebag with about the same weight, since an uneven load can cause the motorcycle to pull to one side, and warns that overloading may also cause the bags to catch in the wheel or chain.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.38, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: Why does the manual recommend fastening a load with elastic cords that have more than one attachment point per side, rather than rope?
choice_a: Rope is actually the stronger and more reliable choice for securing cargo
choice_b: Rope can stretch and knots can come loose, permitting the load to shift or fall, while a loose load could catch in the wheel or chain and lock it up
choice_c: Attachment points have no bearing on how securely a load stays in place
choice_d: Elastic cords are prohibited on public roads
explanation: The manual recommends elastic cords with more than one attachment point per side because rope can stretch and knots can come loose, which could let a load shift or fall, or catch in the wheel or chain and cause it to lock up, resulting in a skid.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.38, 'Tips for Traveling with Passengers and Cargo'

question: Before a long trip with a full load, what does the manual recommend doing on some familiar neighborhood roads?
choice_a: Skipping any test ride, since loading changes nothing about handling
choice_b: Testing the motorcycle unloaded only, then loading it right before the highway trip
choice_c: Taking a test ride with the fully loaded motorcycle to check suspension settings and make sure the side stand, footrests, and exhaust pipes don't scrape
choice_d: Riding as fast as possible to test top speed with the full load
explanation: The manual recommends taking a test ride with the fully loaded motorcycle through familiar neighborhood roads before starting out, to be sure suspension settings are correct and that the side stand, footrests, and exhaust pipes don't scrape over bumps and in turns.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.39, 'Pre-Ride Test'

question: How does a fully loaded motorcycle's acceleration and braking typically compare to an unloaded one, according to the manual?
choice_a: A fully loaded motorcycle accelerates and stops exactly the same as an unloaded one
choice_b: Loading always improves acceleration due to added momentum
choice_c: Loading has no effect on stopping distance, only on top speed
choice_d: Power will be lower, increasing passing times and distances, and braking will feel different with increased stopping distances
explanation: The manual warns that the performance of a fully loaded motorcycle will differ from what riders are used to -- power will be lower, increasing passing times and distances, and braking will feel different, with stopping distances potentially increasing.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.38, 'Pre-Ride Test'
